source.title: Benchmarking Interpretability Tools for Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Stephen Casper; Yuxiao Li; Jiawei Li; Tong Bu; Kevin Zhang; Dylan Hadfield-Menell

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present; no apparent truncation or garbling.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates feature-visualization tools for discovering implanted vision-model trojans. It reports results for visualizing internal neurons, but does not test neuron-pole job counts, held-out activation explanations, attribution graphs, or any other listed claim version.
record.gate_note: The paper reports aggregate human and CLIP results for visualizations of internal neurons and target-class neurons; these bear on neuron-focused interpretability but do not measure any listed version. Other attribution and feature-synthesis results are not rows because they do not measure neuron-pole explanations or the other version-specific claims.
record.test_reason: The paper benchmarks feature-synthesis and attribution tools on recovering implanted trojan triggers in a ResNet50 vision classifier. Its inner-neuron visualization results measure whether humans or CLIP can identify a trojan trigger from visualizations of 10 penultimate-layer neurons. They do not measure how many neurons have one main job, explanation fidelity on held-out activations, simulation scores, or circuit sufficiency, so no version is tested. Neural-network interpretability work is referenced only in passing (feature visualization, network dissection). 'discusses' overstates it, since the paper does not discuss the clean-neuron claim itself; 'cites_only' is closer.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate in part. The authors state that visualizing inner neurons was not effective and was less useful than visualizing the target neuron. They attribute this to trigger recognition being mediated by patterns across multiple neurons, and to inner neurons producing distracting features. The paper's main conclusions are broader. Feature synthesis tools beat attribution/saliency tools on trojan discovery. Robust feature-level adversaries and SNAFUE work best, yet none exceeds 50% human success. Combining tools works best, style trojans are unsolved, and humans are better evaluators than CLIP.
record.recipe_differences: No method from the original neuron-pole audit or the listed claim versions is applied.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported aggregate results differ by visualization parameterization and by whether inner or target-class neurons are visualized; human and CLIP evaluations also differ.

fits_no_version.finding: In a trojaned ResNet50, visualizing the 10 penultimate neurons that most raise the target logit helped humans identify triggers less well than visualizing the target logit neuron. CPPN: 0.24 vs 0.37. Fourier: 0.12 vs 0.12, against a 0.125 chance level.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Visualizations of individual inner neurons are a weak tool for recovering a known model behaviour (a trojan trigger) compared with output-neuron visualization; the authors attribute this to features being mediated by multiple neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: CLIP-based automated matching scored the visualizations lower and less consistently than humans did (inner 0.09/0.18; target 0.06/0.12).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Automated CLIP evaluation of neuron visualizations underperforms human evaluation in trigger recovery.

record.problems: The internal-neuron results are for a vision-model trojan-discovery task and do not measure neuron-pole job counts or explanation fidelity. The paper reports point estimates; it only states that standard error for human proportions is upper-bounded by 0.05. CLIP uncertainty is not stated.
record.rows_left_out: Other feature-attribution and feature-synthesis tool results are omitted because they do not concern neuron-focused interpretations relevant to the claim. Per-trojan values are not included; the rows use the paper's reported aggregate means in Figure 4.

untested.parts: No audit of Qwen3-32B neuron poles or job shares.
No neuron job-share estimates across language models or scales.
No analysis of InceptionV1 polysemantic neurons or pose features.
No interpretable-neuron shares across architectures, regularization or tool quality.
No attribution graphs or replacement-model comparisons.
No comparison of explanations on activating examples versus held-out firing.
No simulation-based scoring of neuron explanations.

record.verdict_notes: Nothing in the paper bears directly on any version. The authors' remark that features are mediated by multiple neurons rather than single ones is a speculative interpretation of a trojan-recovery result, not a measurement of polysemanticity or neuron-job shares. It should not be read as a challenge to V1–V4. Figure 4 shows high per-trojan variance, e.g. Inner Fourier CLIP scores 0.83 on the Sandwich trojan.

versions.untested_parts: Does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles or estimate shares of poles with one job, related jobs, or unknown jobs.
Does not measure neuron-pole job shares across models, architectures, or scales.
Does not analyze InceptionV1 cat-and-car neurons, pose, or recursive generalization.
Does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares across architectures, regularization choices, or tool quality.
Does not evaluate attribution graphs, model-behavior reconstruction, or replacement-model error.
Does not test explanations on activating examples versus held-out firing examples.
Does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text.
